clips.text: You wake up, open your mouth — and a stranger’s accent comes out.
clips.image: Close-up of brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie at a bathroom mirror at dawn, his hand at his throat, mouth open mid-word in shock, face clearly visible, warm dawn gold sunrise light, deep slate ink shadows, high contrast, cinematic, no text
clips.note: AUTOPSY: hook sentence 1 ONLY (~5s); ACTION/AFTERMATH image (mirror shock), face visible, high contrast; aggressive zoom-punch; 350ms pause after a1; bed in after this sentence

clips.text: Only about 100 people in history have ever lived it.
clips.image: PAYOFF FLASH (fresh image, NOT a diagram crop): extreme close-up of a man's open mouth mid-word, golden sound-wave ribbons fracturing and scattering in the air in front of him, deep slate ink background, warm dawn gold light, dramatic, no text
clips.note: AUTOPSY: payoff flash lands ~5s (a genuinely DIFFERENT dramatic image from a1); this IS the twist visual — c8 reuses this exact asset

clips.text: Next: the call nobody believed, the machine behind an accent, the cases since 1907 — and your turn.
clips.image: Split triptych feel in one frame: a ringing phone on a bedside table, a glowing brain with gold sound-waves, an old 1907 newspaper page, warm dawn gold sunrise light, deep slate ink shadows, deep slate ink background, warm gold accents, no text
clips.note: AUTOPSY: re-orientation TIGHT — 19 words, ~7.3s spoken (<= ~8s); music fades in ONLY after a1's first spoken sentence

clips.text: It starts on an ordinary morning. You stand at the bathroom mirror, half asleep, and you say good morning to yourself — except the voice that comes back is not yours. The vowels stretch in the wrong places. The music of the sentence is wrong.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie standing at a bathroom mirror at dawn, saying good morning to his reflection, his expression shifting from sleepy to confused, warm dawn gold sunrise light, deep slate ink shadows, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: open loop 1 (mini): tease overlay + push-in; keyword pop 'NOT YOUR VOICE'

clips.text: You call your mother, and she goes quiet. Then she asks who this is. You say it is you, and she says no, it is not — because the daughter she knows does not sound like a stranger from another country.
clips.image: A young woman holding a phone to her ear in a dawn-lit kitchen, her face falling as the person on the other end goes quiet, warm dawn gold sunrise light, deep slate ink shadows, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: You have never learned another language. You have never lived anywhere else. You cannot speak the language of the accent you now carry — you can only sound like it. And nobody believes that, either.
clips.image: A passport lying open on a kitchen table beside a phone, a plane ticket untouched, dawn light across the table, warm dawn gold sunrise light, deep slate ink shadows, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: uncertainty boundary: patients do NOT gain a new language, vocabulary or grammar

clips.text: About 100 people in history have ever lived this — fewer than the crowd at a school play. And the reason starts with a machine inside your head you never knew you had. That is the call nobody believed.
clips.image: A small school auditorium at dawn, rows of empty seats with one single seat glowing warm gold, warm dawn gold sunrise light, deep slate ink shadows, cinematic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 2: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser; rule 15: case count visualised as an auditorium

clips.text: Chapter two: the identity crisis. Your voice is the sound people use to know it is you — and overnight, that sound belongs to someone else.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie looking at his own reflection in a dark window at dawn, his face doubled and unfamiliar, warm dawn gold sunrise light, deep slate ink shadows, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter card

clips.text: At the hospital, they check your passport first. Not your brain — your passport. Because the simplest explanation is that you are lying about who you are.
clips.image: A doctor at a hospital desk holding up a passport under a bright lamp, a patient waiting across the desk, dawn light through the window, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: An Gie Yen, a dentist in Brisbane, woke from tonsil surgery in 2021 speaking with an Irish accent. She posted videos of it on TikTok. Strangers called her a hoax — thousands of them, in the comments, in her face.
clips.image: A young woman dentist filming herself on a phone in her kitchen at dawn, speaking to the camera, comments floating on the phone screen, warm dawn gold sunrise light, deep slate ink shadows, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: real case: An Gie Yen, 2021; keyword pop 'CALLED A HOAX'

clips.text: That is the second wound. The first is losing your voice. The second is losing the right to be believed — because an accent is not just a sound. It is a claim about where you come from.
clips.image: A close-up of a hand holding an identity card beside a face in shadow, the card photo and the real face not matching, deep slate ink background, warm gold accents, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Michelle Myers, from Arizona, went to bed with a headache in 2015 and woke up British. She had never left the United States. Not once. Her own children asked why their mother suddenly sounded like a stranger.
clips.image: A mother in an Arizona kitchen at dawn talking to her two children, the children staring at her in confusion, warm morning light, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: real case: Michelle Myers, 2015 (reported 2018)

clips.text: And the accent does not even stay still. For Myers, British slid into Australian, then Irish, like a radio drifting between stations. Same mouth, same brain — a different stranger every few months.
clips.image: An old radio on a kitchen table at dawn, its tuning dial drifting between three glowing station markers, warm dawn gold sunrise light, deep slate ink shadows, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: So the question is not how she learned an accent. It is why her brain started filing her own voice under foreign. And the answer is not what you think. That is the laboratory.
clips.image: A filing cabinet drawer sliding open at dawn, one folder inside glowing warm gold and labelled with a sound-wave, deep slate ink background, warm gold accents, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 3: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser

clips.text: Chapter three: the laboratory. An accent is not words. It is timing — and your brain runs the timing on a machine you cannot see.
clips.image: A modern laboratory at dawn, a scientist looking at a glowing gold waveform on a screen, a brain model on the bench, warm dawn gold sunrise light, deep slate ink shadows, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter card

clips.text: Think of your speech as five dials, all turning at once: the timing of each syllable, the rise and fall of your pitch, where your tongue sits, how long each vowel lasts, and how hard each consonant lands. Turn one dial, and you sound tired. Turn all five, and you sound foreign.
clips.image: Five glowing gold dials on a dark slate control panel, each dial turned to a different position, a sound-wave running across the panel, deep slate ink background, warm gold accents, scientific visualization, no text
clips.note: rule 15: the five dials visualised as a control panel

clips.text: The machine lives mostly in the left half of your brain — Broca's area, which plans the movements, the insula, which times them, and the basal ganglia, which keep the rhythm steady. Damage any one of them, and the dials slip.
clips.image: A glowing anatomical view of the left half of a human brain at dawn, three regions lit in warm gold, a sound-wave flowing between them, deep slate ink background, warm gold accents, scientific visualization, no text

clips.text: About 70 percent of cases follow a stroke — a clot or a bleed that starves a small patch of that machine. The rest follow head injuries, migraines, multiple sclerosis, surgery on the mouth or face — or, in some cases, no clear cause at all.
clips.image: A close-up of a blood vessel with a small clot blocking the flow, a patch of brain tissue dimming from gold to grey beside it, deep slate ink background, warm gold accents, scientific visualization, no text
clips.note: uncertainty boundary: ~70% is an estimate, not a census; count-up pop '70%'

clips.text: The mechanism has four moves. First: the sound. Every word you speak is a wave — air, shaped by your tongue, your lips, your breath, rising and falling like a line drawn in the air.
clips.image: ONE speech-machine asset, full view: a human head in profile with golden sound-waves flowing from the mouth, three glowing speech areas inside the brain, deep slate ink background, warm dawn gold light, scientific illustration style, NO text, NO labels, NO letters
clips.note: dataScene beat 1 of 4: staged reveal, one asset; c6-c7 are true crops of this

clips.text: Second: the timing. Your brain spaces the sounds like notes on a score — a fraction of a second early here, a fraction late there — and that spacing is what your ear reads as an accent.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the c5 speech-machine asset, zoomed into the sound-wave zone: golden sound-waves flowing from the mouth with uneven spacing between the peaks, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 2: true crop of c5 asset

clips.text: Third: the brain. The speech areas send the orders, and the muscles obey. When the orders arrive scrambled, the muscles still obey — they just play the notes in the wrong order.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the c5 speech-machine asset, zoomed into the brain zone: three glowing speech areas inside the brain connected by gold threads, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 3: true crop of c5 asset

clips.text: Fourth: the filing cabinet. Your own brain hears the changed pattern and files it under foreign — because that is the closest drawer it has. You have not learned a new accent. You have lost the sound of yourself. That is the cases.
clips.image: PAYOFF FLASH asset reused (a2): extreme close-up of a man's open mouth mid-word, golden sound-wave ribbons fracturing and scattering in the air in front of him, deep slate ink background, warm dawn gold light, dramatic, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 4 = TWIST; reuses the a2 image (NOT a crop of c5 — see Known deviations); chapter-end open loop 4

clips.text: Chapter four: the cases. This has been happening for more than a century — and the first case was written down in Paris, in 1907.
clips.image: A 1907 doctor's study in Paris at dawn, a doctor in a dark suit writing in a leather notebook by lamplight, a patient portrait on the desk, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter card

clips.text: A Parisian man had a stroke, and when he spoke again, he sounded Alsatian — from a region he had never lived in. The doctor who wrote it down was Pierre Marie, and the date is still argued about: some sources say 1901. The count itself is argued about, too.
clips.image: A Parisian man in 1907 clothes speaking in surprise to a doctor, a map of France with Alsace glowing gold on the wall behind them, lamplight, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: uncertainty boundary: first case dated 1907 by most sources, one source says 1901; case count varies (~100 vs ~200)

clips.text: The record has four marks. First: 1907 — Pierre Marie describes the first case, a Parisian man who wakes from a stroke sounding like a stranger from Alsace.
clips.image: ONE timeline asset, full view: a horizontal timeline from 1907 to 2024 on a deep slate ink background, four glowing gold milestones rising along it, a small sound-wave motif at each milestone, scientific diagram style, NO text, NO labels, NO letters
clips.note: dataScene beat 1 of 4: staged reveal, one asset; d4-d6 are true crops of this

clips.text: Second: 2015 — Michelle Myers of Arizona goes to bed with a headache and wakes up British, then Australian, then Irish, without ever leaving the United States.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the d3 timeline asset, zoomed into the second milestone zone: a glowing gold milestone with a small house motif, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 2: true crop of d3 asset

clips.text: Third: 2021 — An Gie Yen, a dentist in Brisbane, wakes from tonsil surgery with an Irish accent, and documents it on TikTok while strangers call her a fake.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the d3 timeline asset, zoomed into the third milestone zone: a glowing gold milestone with a small phone motif, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 3: true crop of d3 asset

clips.text: Fourth: 2024 — Althia Bryden of London wakes from stroke surgery with an Italian accent, though she has never been to Italy. One hundred and seventeen years after the first case — and the count still stands at only about 100 people.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the d3 timeline asset, zoomed into the whole-timeline zone: all four glowing gold milestones along the timeline, a dawn sun glowing above the last one, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 4; keyword pop '117 YEARS'

clips.text: There are others. Lisa Alamia woke from jaw surgery speaking British. Reuben Nsemoh woke from a coma speaking Spanish. Sarah Colwill has lived with it for fifteen years — long enough to watch her own voice become a stranger she got used to.
clips.image: Three portraits side by side at dawn: a woman after jaw surgery, a man waking in a hospital bed, a woman speaking calmly into a microphone, warm dawn gold sunrise light, deep slate ink shadows, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: real cases: Alamia, Nsemoh, Colwill (15 years with FAS)

clips.text: It is reported more often in women — but nobody has settled why. And whether it lasts is a lottery: some cases fade in months, some last for life, and speech therapy helps some people, not all.
clips.image: A woman standing at a dawn-lit window, her reflection showing two overlapping faces, one familiar and one strange, warm dawn gold sunrise light, deep slate ink shadows, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: uncertainty boundary: reported more often in women, reason not settled; permanence varies; therapy helps some

clips.text: So we know the cases, and we know the machine. But the question nobody asks is the one that matters most: if it happened to you tomorrow — which accent would you hope for? That is the test.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie standing at a crossroads at dawn, one road lit by warm Italian sunlight, the other by cool British morning light, warm dawn gold sunrise light, deep slate ink shadows, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 5: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser

clips.text: Chapter five: the test. You have heard the morning, the phone call, the laboratory, and the cases. Now the choice is yours.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie standing at a crossroads at dawn, a map in his hand, two roads ahead, warm dawn gold sunrise light, deep slate ink shadows, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter card

clips.text: Close your eyes and pick. Italian — warm, musical, the accent of long dinners and open windows? Or British — crisp, polite, the voice of every period drama you have ever loved?
clips.image: Split triptych feel in one frame: a long Italian dinner table at sunset, a British period-drama drawing room, an open window with dawn light, warm dawn gold sunrise light, deep slate ink shadows, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Here is the catch nobody tells you: you do not get to pick. The accent picks you — or rather, the damage picks it, and the listeners around you name it. Americans hear British. Britons hear Italian. The same damaged speech, heard by different ears.
clips.image: Two listeners facing each other across a table at dawn, one hearing a British accent and one hearing an Italian accent, a sound-wave between them splitting into two colours, warm dawn gold sunrise light, deep slate ink shadows, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: keyword pop 'THE ACCENT PICKS YOU'; mechanism: accent is perceived, depends on the listener's ears

clips.text: And there is a second catch. You would not gain a language — only the sound of one. You could not order coffee in Rome, or argue in Paris. You would sound Italian and understand nothing. That is the cruelest part: the accent is a costume with nobody inside it.
clips.image: A man standing in a Rome cafe at dawn holding a coffee cup, smiling politely while a menu in Italian stays unreadable to him, warm morning light, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: uncertainty boundary: patients do NOT acquire a new language

clips.text: So here is the question the story turns on: if your voice left you tomorrow — would you miss the sound of yourself, or the person everyone thought you were?
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie alone on a rooftop at dawn, looking out over the city waking up under a gold sunrise, thoughtful, warm dawn gold sunrise light, deep slate ink shadows, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: RHETORICAL-QUESTION beat: slower drift + music duck; 1.75s full silence after (gap)

clips.text: There is no right answer. There is only the answer you would give — and it says something about how much of you lives in your voice. Which brings us to today. That is the choice.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie walking toward the camera at sunrise, blue hoodie, dawn gold light behind him, a city street waking up, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 6: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser

clips.text: One more thing before today: this is not a party trick, and it is not a performance. A sudden change in speech can mean a stroke — and a stroke needs a doctor in minutes, not days. Remember that, and we are ready.
clips.image: A phone on a bedside table at dawn showing an emergency call screen, a hand reaching for it urgently, warm dawn gold sunrise light, deep slate ink shadows, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: medical boundary: sudden speech change needs a doctor urgently (can signal a stroke); not medical advice

clips.text: Chapter six: today. You still speak in your own voice, still hear yourself the way you always have. Nothing about you has changed — except now you know how easily it could.
clips.image: Sunrise over a quiet street, brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie standing outside his house, blue hoodie, dawn gold light on his face, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter card

clips.text: Remember the numbers: about 100 people in history, about 70 percent after a stroke, one machine with five dials, and one morning — the time between your voice and a stranger's.
clips.image: A glass of water on a windowsill at sunrise beside a coiled glowing gold thread, dark room, warm dawn light, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: rule 15: numbers visualised; 'about' per uncertainty boundary

clips.text: And remember the twist: the enemy was never a language you learned. It was the timing inside your own head, slipping by fractions of a second. It was never an accent at all.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie smiling in a bright laboratory at dawn, scientists working behind him, a glowing gold waveform model on the bench, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: keyword pop 'NEVER AN ACCENT'; differentiator stated plainly

clips.text: If you woke up tomorrow speaking with an accent you never learned — what would be the first thing you'd say, and who would you call first? Tell us why.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie looking straight at camera, blue hoodie, dawn gold light on his face, deep slate ink background, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: COMMENT QUESTION (locked, verbatim): 1.5s VO pause + deeper bed duck after

clips.text: Science note, plainly: about 100 cases is a reported count, not a census — some counts say around 200; the first case is dated 1907, though one source says 1901; the 70-percent stroke figure is an estimate, not a census; and whether it lasts varies from person to person.
clips.image: Calm deep slate ink panorama with a single glowing gold thread stretched across an empty field at dawn, vast and peaceful, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: uncertainty recap, explicit

clips.text: The named sources, so you can check me: Pierre Marie, 1907, on the first case; Professor Nicholas Miller of Newcastle University, the leading researcher on this; and the BBC Discovery podcast on waking up with a different voice, with Althia Bryden and Sarah Colwill.
clips.image: Lab notebook and a brain model on a desk, a glowing gold thread across the pages, warm lamp light, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: rule 24: named sources in VO

clips.text: You wake up, open your mouth — and a stranger's accent comes out. The next time you speak without thinking, you will not even notice. Now you know what that freedom is worth.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie walking away along a dawn-lit street, his shadow long in the gold light, cinematic wide shot, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: closing line; logical loop back to the opening hook; keyword pop 'NOW YOU KNOW'

clips.text: Your voice is yours — until one morning, it isn't. Goodnight. And if your voice ever changes overnight — call a doctor first, and tell us second.
clips.image: A sunrise over a quiet city, gold light breaking over rooftops, a single sound-wave fading into the dawn sky, cinematic wide shot, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: closing echo of the reversal title; keyword pop 'UNTIL ONE MORNING'; hold on final frame
